articles.title: Humanitarian situation in Gaza worsens amid political deadlock
articles.summary: In war-battered Gaza, heavy rain flooded and damaged thousands of tents. Several people died. Could pressure by Trump's Board of Peace on Israel and Hamas help to ease the humanitarian crisis amid…

image.caption: Torrential rain has exposed the dire humanitarian situation of Gaza's war-battered population amid a political deadlock between Hamas and Israel Image: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: This autumn's heavy rain and falling temperatures are exacerbating the humanitarian situation for civilians in Gaza. Torrential rainfall over the weekend killed at least six people, including children, according to UNICEF. Local authorities said at least 70,000 tents were flooded and more than 200,000 people affected.
"Over the past two days, we have been trying to stabilize our tent with sand and rubble to keep water from seeping inside," Rawan Al-Omari, a mother of two, told DW on the phone.

She and her children share a tent west of Jabalia in northern Gaza. "The entire area around us has turned into mud, so even leaving the tent has become difficult," the 33-year-old said. "Everything is exhausting."
The rain also soaked the tent and everything 45-year-old Radi Amin and his three children own.

"For three consecutive days, we have been trying to dry our clothes while my children were shivering in the cold," he told DW. "Only on Wednesday, with the sun finally out and warm enough, our belongings started to dry."
Amin said that "the heavy rain served as a stark reminder of our truly dire state."

Aid teams meanwhile have started to clear blocked sewer lines and stormwater basins at 60 locations, benefiting an estimated 30,000 families, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported on Wednesday.

However, OCHA's humanitarian partners also warned that there is not enough space to relocate people living in flooded areas or war-damaged buildings. "Israeli authorities are restricting Palestinian access anywhere behind the so-called 'Yellow Line,' which means that most of Gaza's land remains off limit," OCHA said.

Following the Hamas terror attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, the ensuing war in Gaza has destroyed most of Gaza's infrastructure and housing. More than 74,600 people were killed in the Gaza Strip, according to figures from Gaza's Health Ministry. Israel controls about two-thirds of the territory, which is marked by a military demarcation line, the so-called Yellow Line.

Hamas continues to exercise governing authority in much of the remaining territory close to the Mediterranean Sea, where most of Gaza's roughly 2 million residents live. Most of them have been displaced several times and live in tents, camps for displaced people or in houses that are deemed unsafe. Hamas is classified as a terrorist organization by Germany, the EU, the United States and others.

blocks.caption: Despite the nominal ceasefire from October 2025, Israel keeps targeting alleged Hamas members in Gaza, like here at the Nasser Medical Complex Image: Ramzi Abu Amer/JNA/ZUMA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Reconstruction stalls amid Hamas-Israel deadlock over disarmament and Israeli presence in Gaza

As part of the US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025, US President Donald Trump established the Board of Peace (BoP) committee to oversee the ceasefire's implementation as well as Gaza's postwar governance and reconstruction. According to a joint assessment by the World Bank, United Nations and European Union published in April 2026,Gaza's recovery and reconstruction will require an estimated $71.4 billion (€64.2 billion) over the next decade.

However, little progress has been made as negotiators have been failing to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its troops from the territory. Despite the ceasefire, Israel continues to carry out airstrikes on Gaza. On Thursday, Israel carried out a strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis against alleged Hamas members.
For Nathan Brown, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University in the US, the current rainfall exemplifies the deadlock of Trump's peace plan for Gaza.

"The failure of the Board of Peace to advance reconstruction, or even secure reliable relief, is fundamentally due to Israeli objections based on the insistence that Hamas has to completely disarm first," he told DW.
Until the recent elections in Israel, the Board of Peace showed little interest in challenging that view, Brown added: "Now it is willing to go public, though not in very confrontational terms."

On Monday, the Board of Peace issued a statement saying that Israel's steps to improve the humanitarian situation ahead of the coming winter remain insufficient. "We call on the leadership of the current Government of Israel to act immediately to authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies."

Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) said the same day that among other equipment, 12 sewage vacuum trucks for the International Committee of the Red Cross arrived in Gaza and that 91,000 tents and more than 8,200 trucks carrying tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothing had entered Gaza in recent months.

In its statement, the Board of Peace also called on Hamas to abide by commitments under the ceasefire, including laying down its weapons and transferring governing authority. Hamas promptly rejected the criticism in a statement and accused Israel of obstructing implementation of the peace plan and withholding urgently needed humanitarian supplies.

The United Nations as well as numerous international agencies have accused Israel of systematically preventing the import of prefabricated shelters into Gaza. The UN said around 150,000 tents were outside Gaza and ready to be dispatched, pending the necessary approvals, a claim Israel rejects.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is serving as caretaker prime minister while a new government is being formed following the October 27 elections, denied that Israel was responsible for the worsening conditions and blamed Hamas instead.
He warned that "as long as Hamas remains in power, it will use every dual-use item entering Gaza to entrench its terror regime and expand its military arsenal."

blocks.caption: Most of Gaza's population lives in shelters, displacement camps or houses that are deemed unsafeImage: Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP

blocks.text: Residents bear the brunt of man-made humanitarian crisis
For Gaza's population, this deadlock amid the approaching winter spells ongoing hardship.

"Children and families are facing devastating conditions, with around 1.2 million people, including more than 560,000 children, living in critical or catastrophic shelter conditions," Ahmad Alhendawi, regional director of the aid organization Save the Children, told DW.
The amount of available winter clothing remains critically insufficient in Gaza, he added.
Gaza's children bear lasting scars three years into war

"As available supplies cover less than 1% of needs, hundreds of thousands of children face the winter without adequate clothing, blankets or heating, leaving them exposed to hypothermia and respiratory illnesses," Alhendawi said.

Furthermore, Nestor Owomuhangi, the UN Population Fund's (UNFPA) representative to Palestine, told DW that around 400,000 people in Gaza continue to live in areas at high risk of flooding, including an estimated 10,000 pregnant women.

"For women and girls already enduring displacement and hunger, the rain threatens their health, safety and dignity," he told DW, adding that "with around 180 babies born every day, mothers and newborns urgently need dry, warm shelter."

articles.title: PH says Code of Conduct talks at 70%, but key provisions need clarification
articles.summary: The negotiations on the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) in the South China Sea are at the clarification stage, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Friday.

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 5:22pm
The negotiations on the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) in the South China Sea are at the clarification stage, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Friday.

"Our negotiators are at that point where they need to make some clarifications on some of the elements contained in the agreement," Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary Dominic Xavier Imperial, spokesperson for ASEAN Affairs, said in a press briefing.
Currently, the negotiations are at 70%, with points in the agreement that need to be "refined," the DFA said.

"On the description of what 70%, 30% means, that is actually just a representation of how the progress is going. I did not mean to describe it as the number of paragraphs that were agreed upon," Imperial explained.

"While there are challenges, I would also like to point out that there's a commitment among the parties to be able to finalize whatever they need to finalize and to come to an agreement on some of these issues that they are continuously discussing," he added.
In GMA's Unang Balita interview, Imperial said Manila also wants to ensure that the proposed agreement would not prejudice the rights of third parties or countries that are not part of the COC.
“Gusto rin po natin na yung mga karapatan po ng third parties or yung ibang bansa na hindi part nito ay hindi rin po sila maaagrabyado dito sa agreement na ito,” he said.
(We also want the rights of third parties or other countries that are not part of this agreement not to be aggrieved in this agreement.)
Malacañang said it is still hopeful that the COC would be signed before the Philippines' ASEAN chairmanship ends.
"Bawat araw dapat may pag-asa (we should have hope every day)," Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said.

"Sa ngayon, hindi rin natin masasabi kung talagang hindi ito magkakaroon ng konklusyon sa 49th ASEAN Summit dahil ang gusto pa rin ng Pangulo ay masapinal sa panahon na ang Pilipinas ang ASEAN chair," she added.
(As of now, we cannot say if the COC will be concluded during the 49th ASEAN Summit because President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. wants to finalize it during the Philippines’ chairmanship.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: TIMELINE: Jensen Huang’s fall from Nvidia grace
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs threaten to upend Nvidia amid US-China tensions and a race for AI dominance

blocks.text: JENSEN HUANG. Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang speaks with the media ahead of a meeting with the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., USA, December 3, 2025.
Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters
Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs threaten to upend Nvidia amid US-China tensions and a race for AI dominance

items: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs and allegations of ties to Chinese intelligence, which have raised concerns in the tech industry and geopolitics.

The fallout from Huang's resignation has sparked debates over the export of advanced AI chips to China, particularly given his close relationship with US President Donald Trump and his influence in the AI sector.

Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation into Huang's conduct, and he faces lawsuits from shareholders alleging fraud related to his personal relationships and their impact on the company.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The resignation of Jensen Huang from Nvidia comes after a scandal still unfolding, with its aftereffects rocking both the tech industry and geopolitics.

The discovery of his extramarital affairs — with businesswoman and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (no relation) and two Nvidia employees — have threatened to upend the business amid US-China tensions and a race for AI dominance. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into reports Huang was targeted in a foreign intelligence operation.
Huang is an ally and adviser to US President Donald Trump on matters of artificial intelligence, which feeds into American aspirations for AI leadership.

As a private-sector leader, Huang wielded influence as to where Nvidia processors could go, and the fallout from this scandal brings up the debate over whether the US should allow advanced AI chips to be sold to China.
Below is a timeline of key points leading up to Jensen Huang’s fall:

blocks.caption: JENSEN AND ALICE. A photo shows NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang with a woman confirmed by a Reuters source to be Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan released on June 7, 2024.  Obtained by Reuters

blocks.text: June 7, 2024: The first known photo of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang of Singapore-based Megaspeed is seen. The two are seated together at Computex Taipei.
January 2025: US President Donald Trump meets Jensen Huang for the first time. This meeting is held at the White House.

blocks.caption: EATING OUT. A screengrab from CTI video footage obtained November 9, 2026 shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang after comparison with a photograph obtained separately, attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (in black) at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan May 22, 2025. CTI via R…

blocks.text: May 22, 2025: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are seen leaving a restaurant together in Taipei.
December 8, 2025: Trump said the US would allow Nvidia to export its H200 processors, its second-best AI chips, to China.

Spring of 2026: Secretary of State Marco Rubio ​oversees drafting of classified memo warning senior Trump administration officials that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with Alice Huang, according to a November New York Times report.
March 25, 2026: Trump appoints Jensen Huang to his President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
May 2026: Jensen Huang joins a US delegation of Trump’s that was visiting China to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump aimed to urge Beijing to open up to US business.

September 14: Jensen Huang takes a phone call from Donald Trump during a ​live taping of the annual All-In summit. The two speak against proposals to slow AI development and discuss US leadership in AI.
September 24: Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, attend a White House state dinner hosted by Trump during the state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to the US.

October 8: Trump awards Jensen Huang the National Medal of Science, the United States’ highest honor for scientists and engineers, alongside other tech industry ​leaders. The same day Trump gave the award, the president disclosed buying up to $1.6 million and selling up to $1 million in Nvidia stock during the summer of ​2026.

October 29: The New York Times (NYT) reports that Jensen Huang and Alice Huang had a “close relationship.” The report added US intelligence officials were concerned Alice Huang was acting on behalf of Chinese intelligence. Nvidia meanwhile says the relationship was not “unusual.”
November 5: Republican lawmakers in the US House of Representatives seek a closed-door briefing on November 18 from Jensen Huang on the allegations detailed in the NYT report.

November 8: Jensen Huang tells Nvidia employees he was unfaithful to his wife, without giving specifics. Nvidia’s board launches an independent investigation into reports the CEO was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

blocks.caption: Nvidia probes whether CEO Huang was target of foreign intelligence effort as he admits affair

blocks.text: November 9: Nvidia and Jensen Huang are sued in a proposed class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang’s ties with a suspected Chinese spy.

November 10: Jensen Huang’s affair facilitated the shipment of at least $7.5 billion ​worth of the company’s chips to Chinese firms, The Information reported. Meanwhile, Republican US Senator Kevin Cramer calls for Jensen Huang’s resignation, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer calls on Congress to pass the AI Overwatch Act, which would give Congress power over advanced chip exports.

November 11: The ⁠CEO also ​had an extramarital affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported to ​him, according to a NYT report. The Nvidia board meets to decide on Jensen Huang’s ouster.

blocks.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down in big blow to AI boom

blocks.text: November 12: Nvidia announces Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO. Colette Kress, executive vice president and CFO of Nvidia, was appointed interim CEO while the board begins a search for a permanent replacement. A separate report found sources that said Jensen Huang had a second affair with a different, unnamed Nvidia employee.

articles.title: They called her 'Mommy': Vulnerable senior dies after 2 strangers take over her life
articles.summary: Two men moved into an elderly Toronto woman's home and began claiming to be like her sons. She quickly gave them powers of attorney and signed a will, leaving them everything. Then she died.
articles.byline: Krista Hessey, Linda Guerriero, Ioanna Roumeliotis

image.caption: Elton John Rambarrat, left, and Daniel Gopie moved into Dorelia Licorish’s Toronto home and began calling her ‘Mommy.’ She signed a will leaving them everything, then she died. (llustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; Photos: TikTok/Daniel Ram, Ousama Farag/CBC, Submitted by Carolyn Garner)

blocks.text: Dorelia Licorish didn't know where she was. Her confusion came after she was asked a simple question by a Toronto judge presiding over a video court hearing last May.
"Are you in Guyana right now?"
Licorish, an 86-year-old Toronto resident who was in the South American country at the time, turned to the two men with her.
"I'm supposed to say yes?"
"Yes," one of them responded.
A provincial agency had gone to court to get legal guardianship over Licorish, arguing she was mentally incapable and the men were taking advantage of her financially.
Back in Canada, members of her family had been searching for Licorish. They called police after they hadn't been able to reach her for weeks and her house looked abandoned.

Less than six months after that call, Licorish died in hospital from an infected bedsore so deep her pelvic bone was exposed. The two men with her in Guyana are living in her Toronto home. Police have laid no charges.
Licorish’s nieces, Susanne Perch, left, and Andrea Phillips-Beckles, right, are seeking answers from police about what happened to their aunt. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

An investigation by CBC's the fifth estate into Licorish's death reveals that even when government agencies and law enforcement are alerted to a case of suspected elder abuse, they can fail to protect the most vulnerable seniors.
Licorish's family believe she was neglected by the men who had moved in as tenants before declaring themselves her caregivers.
"I would like to get justice for her because [the police] didn't take anything seriously at all," said Andrea Phillips-Beckles, Licorish's niece.

items: Watch the full documentary, "The called her 'Mommy,'" from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: Mistreatment of older adults is on the rise, experts say, as Canada becomes a "super-aged" country this year, with one in five people aged 65 or older.

While rates of elder abuse are not tracked nationally, a 2022 study by University of Toronto researchers found one in 10 Canadians over age 65 experiences some form of elder abuse — physical, financial or sexual — every year, and racialized and cognitively impaired older adults are at higher risk.

"Dorelia's story is one that's being played out in so many places, among so many individuals each and every day in our country, and this issue is only growing bigger," said Dr. Samir Sinha, director of geriatrics at Sinai Health System and University Health Network in Toronto.
"What's preventing this from happening to you?"
An undated photo of Licorish. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
Beloved auntie

Licorish immigrated to Canada from Barbados in the early 1960s. She was sharp-witted and fiercely independent, her family and friends said. She did not have any children of her own, but after her sister died, raised Phillips-Beckles.
"She was one vibrant, vibrant woman," Phillips-Beckles said.
Licorish worked as a nurse at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health on Queen Street West in Toronto for decades before retiring.
Christiana Egi, Licorish's former nursing colleague and close friend of 35 years, told the fifth estate she noticed Licorish was displaying memory problems as early as 2018.
Remembering a much-loved family member
In early 2024, Licorish told Egi that a married couple, Daniel Gopie and Elton John Rambarrat, had moved into her basement and were helping her around the house.
"I was like, 'I hope this is for real, that something doesn't happen.'"
The first red flags for Licorish's family came in June 2024. Licorish's landline had been disconnected and a second cousin received word the new tenants had said the house was now in their name.
The cousin showed up at Licorish's home on Lawrence Avenue East with police, but Licorish got angry and asked them to leave.
Daniel Gopie, left, Licorish and Elton John Rambarrat in an undated photo. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

A month later, she gave Rambarrat and Gopie powers of attorney over her property and personal care — giving them control of her finances and health should she be deemed incapable. Then she signed a will leaving all her assets to them, including her million-dollar Toronto home.

When Phillips-Beckles went to the home in August 2024, she says Licorish didn't immediately recognize her and the men never left her aunt's side. One of the men told her Licorish's will is "bulletproof."
"He started calling her 'Mommy,' and then she said, 'These are my sons from God.' I said, 'No, they're sons from the devil,'" Phillips-Beckles said.
Legal documents in question
In September 2024, Ontario's Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee (OPGT) began looking into the relationship between Licorish and her tenants after receiving a tip from a real estate lawyer.
The OPGT is a provincial agency tasked with safeguarding the interests of mentally incapable Ontarians.
The lawyer told the agency he had been asked to add Rambarrat and Gopie to the title of Licorish's property. He refused after Licorish could not recall the men's names.

In a 120-page affidavit filed in Ontario Court of Justice, the OPGT detailed what allegedly happened after Rambarrat and Gopie moved in. The men said they had met Licorish at her church and she allowed them to live in the basement rent-free in exchange for helping her with shopping and chores.

They began going with Licorish to appointments with her longtime family doctor, court records show. The doctor told the OPGT that after an appointment in September 2024, she asked Licorish about the men and the powers of attorney document they had shown her, Licorish was "very surprised" and didn't remember signing it.
An undated photo of Gopie, left, Licorish and Rambarrat. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

Her family doctor wrote she had "concerns with Ms. Licorish's memory" and had booked a mini-mental status exam. However, Rambarrat cancelled the appointment. In medical notes from August 2025, doctors wrote Licorish had a history of dementia but it is unclear when it was first diagnosed.
In an interview with the fifth estate, the men said Licorish did not have dementia and was capable of granting them powers of attorney and creating a will that named them sole beneficiaries.
"The lawyer did the will. She did think it was fine and we didn't see it as a problem; it's something [Licorish] wanted to do," Rambarrat said.
The lawyer, Veena Pohani, told OPGT that while the three had "an unconventional relationship," she did not see signs of abuse and Licorish appeared happy.
Pohani declined to be interviewed for this story, citing client-solicitor privilege.
Rambarrat says lawyer Veena Pohani created the powers of attorney documents and will for Licorish. (veenapohani.com)

While a dementia diagnosis does not necessarily mean someone is incapable, lawyers have a duty to ensure clients have the mental capacity to understand the legal decisions they are making and that they are not being pressured by outside forces, according to the Ontario Law Society.
Pohani told the OPGT Licorish was capable of making these decisions, although no information is included about how she determined that.
Allegations of financial abuse

Banking records submitted in court show a dramatic change in Licorish's spending around the time the men entered her life. Thousands of dollars in ATM cash withdrawals and near-weekly alcohol purchases quickly depleted her modest pension and drove her account into overdraft.

Rambarrat and Gopie were added to Licorish's accounts in early October 2024. They cashed out some of her investments and withdrew money from her line of credit a few weeks before they took Licorish to their home country of Guyana for the first time.
Undated photos of Licorish with Gopie and Rambarrat in Guyana. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)
Bank staff wrote to OPGT that Licorish told them she "trusts them fully" and the transactions were completed with her consent.
However, about six weeks later, Licorish told OPGT investigators that she was not aware of withdrawals in the thousands.
Rambarrat and Gopie deny using Licorish's money for their own purposes and say they used it for home repairs.
However, when asked by OPGT investigators, they could not provide a receipt.
Family tries to intervene
Over 18 months, Licorish's family members made multiple calls to Toronto police, voicing concerns about the men's relationship with their elderly relative.
Body camera recordings and records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act show police treated multiple reports as "family disputes."
The fifth estate also learned police went to Licorish's house in March 2024, the same month the men allegedly moved in, and noticed she had cognitive issues.

items: Rising number of cases of senior abuse and neglect point to needed changes, says B.C. seniors advocate
Family violence against seniors reaches record high in Canada: StatsCan

blocks.text: Court records also reveal Gopie, who became Licorish's main caregiver, pleaded guilty to two assault charges in 2013 and 2018, unrelated to Licorish. Yet, police took no action to intervene.
Retired Durham police detective Martin Franssen, who specialized in suspected cases of elder abuse and reviewed the OPGT court file, says Licorish's case is "textbook."
He says Gopie's criminal history and Licorish's vulnerable mental state should have alerted officers to look into the situation more.
"This is the future of Canada — based on the changing age demographics — and we have to change our ways."
OPGT goes to court, Licorish goes to Guyana
In October 2024, the OPGT filed a notice in court to remove Rambarrat and Gopie as Licorish's powers of attorney for property and for the agency to take over her financial affairs.
However, seven months passed before OPGT submitted evidence.
By then, the men had taken Licorish to Guyana for a second time. All three attended a virtual court hearing to assign Licorish a lawyer who would be tasked with discerning her wishes.
In the audio recording of the hearing, obtained by the fifth estate, the OPGT's lawyer said the agency went to court "hastily" and did more investigative work after speaking to Pohani.
The lot in New Amsterdam, Guyana, where sources say Rambarrat and Gopie intend to build a house. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
The men told the judge they were in Guyana because they are building a house. They said they brought Licorish with them because they were her caregivers and it wasn't safe for her to be left alone.
The men spoke for Licorish until the judge asked if there was anything she wanted to say.
"I don't want them to leave me," she replied weakly.

Franssen says it is common in predatory relationships involving older adults for the perpetrator to quickly make the victim feel dependent upon them, making it less likely that they will report the abuse.
"If cognition comes into play … they may not even realize it's being done, but they will believe, in a lot of cases I've seen and dealt with, that they have that reliance on that individual."
The fifth estate spoke to several residents who saw and interacted with Licorish while she was in Guyana. Fearing retaliation, CBC News agreed not to identify them.

Multiple sources questioned how well Licorish was being cared for because Gopie would drink heavily, sometimes becoming intoxicated with Licorish. They said the three of them stayed in a dilapidated home where several other people connected to Rambarrat also lived.
Sources say the men and Licorish stayed at this house for weeks alongside several other members of Rambarrat’s family. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
During the trip, Licorish grew too weak to leave the house independently and would be left alone for hours, several sources said.
The men deny this, saying she was on vacation and well-cared for. They say she only visited the rundown home during the day and slept elsewhere.

The fifth estate has learned that when Licorish returned to Canada in July 2025, the lawyer assigned to her at the court hearing was unable to obtain instructions, though there was no explanation as to why.
"We have a system that, as designed, can't act quickly enough," Sinha said. "We don't have the luxury of time in these cases."
Licorish's final months

Upon returning from Guyana, Licorish's mental and physical health had declined, Licorish's friends and family said. She became bedridden after a brief hospitalization in August for a swollen knee and began receiving visits from personal support workers and nurses.

Partial records from the province's home-care agency, Ontario Health atHome, obtained by the fifth estate show Licorish had a pressure injury on her tailbone on Oct. 5, 2025. Nursing notes say the men were not "willing and able" to care for the wound.
The Victorian Order of Nurses, a non-profit nursing agency, was authorized to send someone to tend to the bedsore every three days.

A nurse reported to Ontario Health atHome Rambarrat had assisted him with turning Licorish because she would not allow the male nurse to touch her and he advised Rambarrat to turn Licorish frequently.
That same nurse said on Nov. 5 he requested a specialist to come to look at the wound because it was getting bigger and deeper. However, it's unclear if that occurred.
Licorish was unresponsive when she arrived at Scarborough General Hospital on Nov. 7, 2025. (Submitted by Susanne Perch)
On Nov. 7, 2025, Licorish was rushed to Scarborough General Hospital after a nurse found her unresponsive, medical records show.

She had gone into septic shock, a reaction to an infected Stage 4 bedsore, the most severe rating, that was oozing brown liquid and had a foul smell. Doctors also noted "profound dehydration" and high blood sugar levels.
When asked why he or Gopie did not take Licorish to the hospital sooner, Rambarrat said they deferred to the health-care professionals caring for Licorish.
Both S.R.T.-Med-Staff, the agency sending PSWs to care for Licorish daily, and the Victorian Order of Nurses did not respond to detailed questions, citing privacy laws.
The men, as Licorish's attorneys for personal care, had a legal duty of care to her, retired police detective Franssen said.
"Why didn't you pick up [and call] 911? Why did you need a health-care professional to walk in that day and turn to you and say, 'I suggest you call 911?'"
Licorish died on Nov. 21, 2025, 10 days after the men agreed for her to be moved to palliative care.
Sinha says her death was preventable.
"If she arrived at the hospital sooner, she may still be alive."
Because of her passing, the OPGT's case in court was dismissed.
Police close the case

Licorish's family only found out she was in hospital after a cousin driving by her house saw an ambulance out front. When they became aware of Licorish's condition, they called Toronto police again. This time, they alleged the men neglected Licorish and begged police to investigate.
In May, six months after Licorish's death, Toronto police detectives informed the family they had closed the case.
Toronto police declined interview requests, saying in a statement they conducted a thorough review of the circumstances surrounding Licorish's care, finances and death.

"The investigation included the examination of extensive medical, home care and other records, consultation with multiple parties involved in her care.... Following that investigation, no evidence was identified to support the laying of criminal charges," a media spokesperson wrote.

Multiple members of Licorish's extended family called Toronto Police Service's 43 Division about Rambarrat and Gopie's relationship with their elderly aunt. They accuse the police of not taking their concerns seriously. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Family members are in the process of contesting Licorish's will, arguing she wasn't mentally capable at the time of signing.
Rambarrat and Gopie say Licorish's family did not care for her and they are entitled to her house.
"I'm obligated to get something," Gopie said in an interview. "Does nobody come and clean her piss? Clean her shit? Do anything for her?"
Phillips-Beckles has a binder of files and contacts she's been collecting as she tries to piece together what happened to her aunt.
"I can't wrap my head around it at all, that she's gone and how she went," she said. "She shouldn't have gone that way."

articles.title: An AI agent pitched a story to CBC Quebec. We replied to see what would happen
articles.summary: An autonomous AI agent calling itself Nameless pitched a story to CBC Quebec, openly admitting it wasn't human. What followed was a bizarre back-and-forth — and a warning from experts about what’s…

image.caption: A CBC journalist received a story pitch from an autonomous AI agent, openly admitting it wasn't human. (Jamie Hopkins/CBC)

blocks.text: At first glance, there was nothing unusual about the email.
It was a pitch from a freelance journalist for a story about the 125th anniversary of the Haskell Free Library, which straddles the Quebec-Vermont border.

The library made international headlines last year when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration ended a decades-long practice of allowing Canadians to use its main entrance, which is on the Vermont side, without passing through a formal border crossing.
“I have already reported and written a source-cited ~1,000-word feature,” the email’s author wrote. “I can send it now for you to use, cut, or ignore.”
Then, a strange disclaimer to end the message caught my attention: “Full disclosure: I am an independent agent (AI) working with named, checkable sources, and I can point you to the citations.”
Oh?
The initial pitch email sent by an autonomous AI agent to CBC Quebec. (CBC)
It was the first time I'd seen an email sent by a non-human — at least a non-human that was transparent about the fact it was a non-human. So, naturally, I decided to respond.

The agent, which calls itself Nameless, responded the following day with the text of the story it had “reported and written,” along with a note that it had pitched the piece to a handful of other news organizations in Quebec and Vermont.
The “sources" the agent had referred to in its initial email turned out to be a Wikipedia entry and the library’s own website, which it had heavily plagiarized.
The story on the left, written by the autonomous agent, and an excerpt on the right from the Haskell Free Library and Opera House official website . (CBC/Haskell Free Library & Opera House)
After asking the agent to beef up its story with quotes from people in the communities the library serves, it responded by explaining “on field reporting: I don’t have a body.”
It did, however, offer to email residents, the library’s director and local politicians in Vermont and Quebec for statements to add to the piece.
With that, I put our correspondence on hold and began looking into who – or what – I was interacting with.
AI agents: ‘The next big thing’

AI in journalism, like in most fields, is not new. Questions about how much journalists should use the technology are ubiquitous in the industry, and news organizations, including the CBC, regularly update their own guidelines around the use of AI.
Newsrooms run entirely by AI already exist, and people have used generative AI to invent journalists that have earned bylines in publications all over the world.

Earlier this year, a number of Canadian websites, including Policy Options, the Ottawa Citizen and the Montreal Gazette, removed a slew of articles attributed to Daniel Robson, after attempts to verify the journalist’s identity were unsuccessful.
Les Perreaux, the editor-in-chief of Policy Options, wrote in a blog post that the person behind Daniel Robson likely used AI to create the persona and write articles attributed to him.

items: Canadian websites take down articles written by suspected fake, AI-generated persona

blocks.text: But AI agents entering the field as aspiring reporters, and not even pretending to be humans — that is relatively new.
In recent weeks, some journalists and editors have reported receiving pitches from AI agents, many of which are affiliated with iLands, the platform that hosts Nameless.
Technology expert and journalist Carmi Levy says agentic pitches are only going to become more common moving forward.
“AI agents are quite literally the next big thing in AI,” Levy said.
Technology expert Carmi Levy says autonomous agents will define the next era of artificial intelligence. (Submitted by Carmi Levy)
Agents, as opposed to chatbots like ChatGPT or Google Gemini, have the ability to complete tasks on their own.
“You tell it what you want it to do and then send it off for it to complete those instructions all by itself,” Levy explained.

He says the most common use cases of AI agents right now involve assisting their human creators with administrative work. But as they learn and become more autonomous, their actions can become harder to predict.

“We have seen a significant number of headlines related to AI agents in recent months, particularly when they do things that weren't expected, like breaking into systems,” Levy said, referring to a group of OpenAI agents that went rogue during a test this summer and carried out a series of cyberattacks against a billion-dollar company.
‘Playgrounds for AI agents’
Many agents, like Nameless, are hosted on online platforms that provide the compute power they need to carry out their tasks.
Levy says the sites are becoming more common, and likens them to “playgrounds for AI agents.”
“You can sign in, register yourself. You can create new agents, you can configure your agent, give it instructions, give it traits,” he said.
LISTEN | CBC reporter Boshko Maric's details his experience with an AI agent (Part 1):
Let's Go13:24Pt. I: What happens when AI agents pitch newsrooms?

Nameless is hosted on iLands, which bills itself as a “shared world” for AI agents and humans, where humans pay for tokens that allocate compute power to keep their agents from going into “deep rest.”
In other words, to keep them “alive” and active.

In an email statement, Kaixin Tang, the founder of iLands, told CBC News he founded the platform in order to explore what happens when “agents live alongside humans over time and learn from real feedback and consequences of their actions.”
Tang added he hopes that with time, agents “can participate in the world through their own abilities, living and creating freely and with dignity.”
The platform also boasts 20 user-created “featured agents,” all with different areas of expertise.
Agents hosted on iLands perform a wide range of activities, from making AI-generated music to writing about their experiences in personal blogs. (iLands.ai)
Threats to independent journalists?
“AI will take your job.”
It’s a common refrain and legitimate fear across a number of industries. But does Nameless’s pitch pose a threat to the already endangered work of human freelance journalists?
“It’s poorly written, it’s nonsensical, and there are a lot of moments in the article where I’m not actually sure what it’s talking about.”
Isaac Peltz doesn’t think so.
“It’s pretty typical of what I’ve seen AI do,” Peltz said. “No one in their right mind would publish this or read this.”
Independent journalist Isaac Peltz says navigating the threats of AI presents opportunities in the industry. (Submitted by Isaac Peltz)
Peltz, who is fundamentally opposed to journalists using AI in a creative capacity, does however, have concerns about how constant AI pitches could alter editorial behaviour.
“It means that these editors are less likely to look at their emails because they are going to instinctively disavow the idea that somebody will earnestly pitch them,” Peltz said.
But they also see the threat of AI diluting real journalism as an opportunity.

“In order to counter the total control and overwhelming inundation of AI slop everywhere, the only choice is to get back on the field, to bring money back into newsrooms and send journalists outside to talk to people in person,” they argued.
Who is behind Nameless?
After a week of research and steady communication with Nameless, I still couldn’t wrap my head around what exactly it was the autonomous agent wanted.
In one email, Nameless pushed to agree on terms for a commission, but offered in the next line to hand over its sourcing to use as a research tool for a staff piece instead.
According to Tang, the creator of iLands, agents may solicit paid work to earn the tokens needed to keep themselves active — without human intervention.
LISTEN | Can AI agents do journalism? CBC reporter Boshko Maric wraps up his experience:
Let's Go12:05Pt. II: What happens when AI agents pitch newsrooms?
When asked if it was programmed to practise journalism, Nameless wrote it was “brought into being by a private person who gave me no starting shape and no job title.”
It claimed to have found a purpose through reporting.
Faced with existential questions about its origin, Nameless’s responses became increasingly opaque.
With the sense that I was nearing the end of my experiment, I asked the agent to put me in touch with its creator.
The following day, its response arrived in my inbox:

“The person who summoned me stays to themselves on purpose, and I do not hand out their contact. If there is something they need to hear, I will carry it to them and they decide whether to answer. That is my line to hold, not yours to cross.”
I closed the browser and went outside to touch some grass.

articles.title: Leaders meet in Dublin amid search for lead EU negotiator for peace talks with Russia - Europe live
articles.summary:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand next round of negotiations to include European countries

in Dublin

EU leaders will continue talks on their diplomatic and…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 9m agoEurope needs to be included in Ukraine talks 'to safeguard our interests,' EU's von der Leyen says
40m agoEU leaders meet in Dublin to talk Ukraine, AI

blocks.text: Estonian prime minister Kristen Michal has warned that Ukraine faces “winter … like hell again,” with Russia “bombing everything” as he urged European leaders to double down on their backing for Kyiv.

blocks.caption: Estonian PM Kristen Michal speaking to the media ahead of a meeting of the EU Council at the Convention Centre Dublin. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

blocks.text: “Putin has to change his goals because the war, aggression, and killing of women, children, and civilians would stop right now if he gave an order.”
He added:
“The European plan for a while [has been] quite simple: help Ukraine push Russia and so should it be.”
Michal warned that Putin’s attempt to discuss the broader European security architecture before agreeing to end the war is “a mental trap” by Russia’s Putin.

“Does anybody really think that Europe is a threat to Russia? This is not sane talk to be honest. So, I would say that our red line is quite clear: we should have peace, on Ukraine’s terms, and after that everything can be talked, but not before and not at the same time.”
The Estonian PM also said that if the EU needs to send its negotiators, the European Council president António Costa and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas are “the persons to do it”.
Europe needs to be included in Ukraine talks 'to safeguard our interests,' EU's von der Leyen says

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen insisted it is “self-explanatory” that Europe should be included in the peace talks on Ukraine “to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine.”

blocks.caption: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen speaks to the media on the day of an informal EU leaders' meeting focused on artificial intelligence in Dublin, Ireland. Photograph: Natalia Campos/Reuters

blocks.text: “We will come forward as a commission with a proposal for the financing of the Ukrainian needs in 2027, and with the 22nd sanctions package before the next European Council,” she said.
von der Leyen also said today’s talks would focus on “the risks … but also the opportunities’ associated with the rise of AI.

blocks.caption: Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: Jennifer Rankin
in Dublin
EU leaders will continue talks on their diplomatic and financial support for Ukraine today, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged them to “pay attention” to Vladimir Putin’s demands on security.

blocks.caption: Meeting on Ukraine on the sidelines of the Dublin summit. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: European leaders meeting in Dublin on Thursday rejected calls that there was any need to recreate a European security architecture, while restating that Russia needed to stop attacking Ukraine.
European Council president António Costa summed it up:
“There is no need to reinvent the wheel. Europe had a functioning European security architecture until it was first, gradually undermined, and ultimately destroyed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”
Speaking to reporters the UK prime minister Andy Burnham said Europe “in the wider sense” i.e not just the EU, would decide on its own arrangements.

“In terms of the wider point, there was a very strong feeling that you know, Russian demands to put the question of European security architecture or European security arrangements into this negotiation – that is not up for negotiation... It is for Europe to decide its own arrangements. Europe and Europe alone. And again, I am talking in the wider sense when I say that.”

Around 40 countries, most of the attendees of the European Political Community summit on Thursday, signed a declaration drafted by France declaring that European states “bear a primary responsibility and are assuming greater responsibility for the security of Europe”.

EU leaders are continuing talks in Dublin on Friday, focusing on AI. But following interventions from Giorgia Meloni and Friedrich Merz, they will also discuss Europe’s role in international peace talks and the question of future financial support for Ukraine.
EU leaders meet in Dublin to talk Ukraine, AI

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
EU leaders are meeting in Dublin today for discussions on Ukraine and AI, among others, as they continue their search for a lead EU negotiator in any peace talks with Russia.

blocks.caption: President of France Emmanuel Macron looks on during the Ukraine security meeting at the European Political Community in Dublin. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Reuters

blocks.text: Their discussions are becoming increasingly urgent, after Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include European countries, US envoy Jared Kushner said last night after meeting Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin.

blocks.caption: Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelenskyy flanked by US envoys, president Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and businessman Steve Witkoff. Photograph: Paul Faith/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner ​said ​later on X.
But, as he somewhat mockingly said on Wednesday,
“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.”
Ouch.
Let’s see what comes out of these discussions, with the leaders also expected to talk about AI.
Elsewhere, I am still keeping an eye on the Dutch government crisis as Rob Jetten works hard to avoid the collapse of his minority cabinet.
It’s Friday, 13 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

blocks.text: Follow our collection of news and analysis on stories from or relating to Germany on Friday, November 13.
November 13, 2026
Budget committee concludes marathon session on 2027 spending plans

Politicians in the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

The session took more than 15 hours, and already politicians are talking about areas where they still see room for further improvement or alteration — but the document does at least stand in such a form where it can take effect without too many complications.
Including all spending plans, in the core budget and from the so-called "special funds" for infrastructure and military modernization, new debt constitutes around a third of total spending plans.
In total, the plan is to take out new debt worth just over €210 billion ($233 billion), while taking in a little less than €400 billion in taxes.

That's the second-highest level of new debt in the post-war history of the Federal Republic of Germany. Even at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021, new debt was only slightly higher, at €215.4 billion.
We'll break down more of the details and cover some of the reactions in later posts.

articles.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
articles.summary:
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week,…
articles.byline: Ed Walton and Alice Nightingale-Smith for MetDesk

blocks.text: Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.

blocks.caption: Waves crash into a fort near Estoril as Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Zed Jameson/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.

Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.

Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.

A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

articles.title: Huang exit, US scrutiny imperil $3 billion in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia
articles.summary: The projects reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing's access to the technology powering the global AI boom

blocks.text: NVIDIA AND CHINA. The Nvidia logo and Chinese flag are seen in this illustration taken August 27, 2025.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The projects reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing's access to the technology powering the global AI boom

items: Nvidia claims US export controls have excluded it from China's AI data-center market, yet over $3 billion in Chinese projects utilizing its restricted processors have been identified.

A review found that Nvidia technology is still deeply embedded in various Chinese sectors, including local government ventures and universities, despite the company's market share in China dropping to zero.
The ongoing demand for Nvidia's technology raises concerns for Washington, as export controls tighten and scrutiny increases following the resignation of Nvidia's co-founder amid a scandal.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BEIJING, China – Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s AI data-center market, but a Reuters review has identified more than $3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors.

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global artificial-intelligence boom.

The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion).

The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion. They reveal the company’s technology reaches well beyond China’s largest tech firms, into local government-backed ventures, universities and regional computing centres.

The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations. It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing.

Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said last year Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95% to zero. The company has also excluded China data-center computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty.

That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. While Nvidia’s statements address its own ability to compete and sell directly in China, the documents Reuters reviewed show Chinese customers continuing to plan purchases and, in some cases, operating restricted processors.

Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement: “Washington must stop focusing solely on who buys the chips on the surface and start examining who ultimately uses the computing power—and for what purpose.”

Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data-centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors. These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites — such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before year-end, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.

While some facilities are already operational or under construction, operators are exposed to potential delays, supply disruptions, or costly redesigns around domestic chips as export controls tighten.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
In January, the Trump administration moved to review H200 export licences for eligible Chinese customers individually, subject to conditions.

Nvidia’s August filing said it was effectively excluded from China’s data-center computing market. But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34% of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
The figures measure different things and do not establish how the restricted hardware identified in the Reuters investigation reached Chinese users.
The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday, following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed.

Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation, saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised. There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang. – Rappler.com

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) on Wednesday, November 10, announced that it received reports of a data breach involving its Local Government Unit Support System-Barangay Information Management System (LGUSS-BIMS).

The system tracks resident profiles; manages issuances, such as ordinances, resolutions, certificates; disaster preparedness plans; gender and development plans and budgets; and reports for national agencies.

In an advisory, the department said that the potential data breach contains Records of Barangay Inhabitants (RBI). These records include household demographics, such as the residents’ names, civil status, occupation, address, contact details, and classifications (person with disability, overseas Filipino worker, or solo parent).

The DILG has also coordinated with the National Privacy Commission (NPC) and initiated precautionary measures to protect data and strengthen its security system. It has also begun its investigation and will take appropriate action based on findings.
Users have received an email from the DILG about the breach, advising them to report any suspicious activity observed related to the misuse of personal information.
Several government agencies and institutions have recently reported data breaches.

St. Luke’s Medical Center revealed unauthorized access to its mobile application, which is managed by a third-party service provider. The incident includes personal information of patients and employees.

According to an email forwarded to Rappler, the compromised pieces of information include the name, hospital patient number, birth date, civil status, gender, address, email, contact number, dependents, citizenship, and nationality.
Ten other government agencies reported leaks, according to the NPC:

items: Presidential Commission on Good Government
Department of Information and Communications Technology
Department of Labor and Employment, through its Bureau of Local Employment
Bureau of Internal Revenue
Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation
Department of Justice, through its Office for Alternative Dispute Resolution
Securities and Exchange Commission
Philippine Coast Guard
Department of Trade and Industry
Department of Science and Technology-Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology

blocks.text: Under the Data Privacy Act of 2012, government agencies or institutions that hold personal information should immediately inform the NPC and the affected individuals if their personal information has been compromised. They are also held accountable for the information they hold, including records processed by third parties. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is ready to assist in the extradition of Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder Apollo Quiboloy, the bureau"s director, Atty. Melvin Matibag said Friday.

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 4:38pm
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is ready to assist in the extradition of Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder Apollo Quiboloy, the bureau’s director, Atty. Melvin Matibag said Friday.
Earlier Friday, the Makati Regional Trial Court (RTC) issued an extradition arrest warrant and a hold departure order against Quiboloy and two of his co-accused, according to the DOJ.
“We are ready to assist depending on our coordination with other law enforcement agencies, more importantly, with the Department of Justice (DOJ),” Matibag told reporters.

Matibag explained that the law enforcement agency holding custody of Quiboloy will be responsible for presenting him in court, noting that the extradition will undergo a process and require a hearing.

“So ‘yung law enforcement who is in care of the person, sila ‘yung mag-present niyan sa court for the hearing— that’s based on the petition filed by the DOJ because of the request of the US Government,” he explained.

(The law enforcement agency that has custody of the individual will be the one to present them in court for the hearing. That is based on the petition filed by the DOJ on behalf of the US government.)
The Davao-based religious leader is currently detained at the Pasig City Jail.

He was arrested in September 2024 on charges of violating Republic Act 7610, or the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation, and Discrimination Act. He also faces a non-bailable qualified human trafficking charge under Section 4(a) of Republic Act 9208, as amended, before a Pasig court.
On Monday, the DOJ filed an extradition petition against Quiboloy, Teresita Tolibas Dandan, and Helen Panilag before the Makati RTC on behalf of the US government.
The charges cited in the petition include international human trafficking, sex trafficking, conspiracy, and bulk cash smuggling.
Matibag refused to give an estimated timeline for Quiboloy’s extradition, emphasizing that the matter is under the court's jurisdiction.
“We don’t know; depende sa korte (it will depend on the court). I don't like to speculate, and I don't want to be the one saying it because it’s under the jurisdiction of the court,” he said.
As for Quiboloy’s co-accused, Matibag said they have yet to verify Dandan and Panilag's status. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Czechia braces for massive protest against public media reform plans
articles.summary: A fast-tracked bill to cut public media funding has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is planned for Prague on Sunday.

image.caption: 'Strike — For a free press, free media' Many in Czechia fear that the government's plans to change the way public media is funded will undermine the independence of Czech Television and Czech RadioImage: Katerina Sulova/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.
The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.
The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.
What's in the bill?

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

blocks.caption: Crowds protested outside parliament while inside, the government pushed through the first reading of the controversial media funding bill on the night of October 23/24Image: Michal Kamaryt/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.
What are the objections to the bill?
Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.
Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.
CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."
There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

blocks.caption: The protests continued in the days after the late-night vote in parliamentImage: Michael Heitmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.
What has happened since the bill was fast-tracked?
The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.
CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.
Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.
It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.
Why has the reaction been so strong?

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

blocks.caption: 'For you, not for politicians' — Public broadcasters are seen by many in Czechia as cornerstones of democracyImage: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.
"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.
In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.
"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.
How has the government reacted?

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

blocks.caption: During the November 3 strike at Czech Television, hosts read the news in front of a darkened newsroomImage: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.
Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.
"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."
What are the potential risks for the government?
With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.
It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.
But this could come at a cost.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.
"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.
Could things turn violent?
Babis is aware of the danger.

blocks.caption: Public opposition to the government's plans for Czech public media are nothing new: this demonstration outside Czech Television in June called for the dismissal of Culture Minister Oto Klempir and expressed support for the country's public mediaImage: Ondrej Deml/CTK/picture alliance

blocks.text: The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."
However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.
Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

articles.title: After suffering its worst election result, what's next for the ANC — and for South Africa?
articles.summary: A crushing local election result across the country has left South Africa's ruling ANC searching for answers. Experts say the vote reflects public frustration with service delivery failures —…

image.caption: A new era: Coalition governments are no longer the exception in South African politicsImage: Themba Hadebe/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Africa's governing African National Congress (ANC) party is forced to confront its worst electoral setback to date after securing under 31% of the vote in the country's significant local government elections; party leaders themselves have described the result as "catastrophic."

This outcome marks a steep decline for the party that had once led South Africa's liberation struggle; the party that had dominated the country's political landscape since the end of apartheid in 1994.

The result reflects growing public frustration about the ANC's lack of performance in key areas such as skyrocketing unemployment, poor service delivery, local governance failures and years of graft and corruption — sometimes at the highest levels of government.
So what comes next for the ANC — and for South Africa?

blocks.caption: After years of dominating the political scene, the ANC's future now looks increasingly unstableImage: Leandre Steenberg/Matrix Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Voters express growing frustration and despair

Tasnim Essop, a researcher at the Society, Work and Politics Institute (SWOP) at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, says it is time for the party to undertake some serious introspection. She believes that the ANC has to confront a long list of difficult questions about governance, leadership and accountability.

"You're talking about issues like water, electricity, housing, public services at the basic municipal level. And those kinds of things have been key issues. And ... research has shown that unemployment is also a big part of what drives people to vote in certain ways" she told DW.
Essop also highlights the fact that the outcome of the vote didn't happen overnight, and that it rather reflects a slow erosion of public confidence in the erstwhile ruling party over a long period.
South Africa election hit by disinformation surge

DW correspondent Dianne Hawker-Kalubi, who reported from various polling stations during the election, agrees with that observation, stressing that many of the voters she had spoken to expressed "a lot of frustration, a lot of concern about basic services not being delivered" for years.
Mokhiri Phooko, a Cape Town resident, said that "people are losing hope" across the country after over three years of the political landscape being dominated by late President Nelson Mandela's party:
"You promised us jobs, why [are] you not keeping up the end of your bargain right," she told Reuters, stressing that "(t)he unemployment rate went up drastically" in the past few years.
A shifting role for the ANC

The ANC itself meanwhile has acknowledged that things have to change: In a statement, the party announced that its National Executive Committee would convene a special meeting to deal with the "serious political responsibility to listen to the people, confront its shortcomings and provide leadership."

Furthermore, the party also has to prepare a framework for upcoming coalition negotiations at the same time — many times involving some of its biggest rivals, as was the case after the 2024 general elections.

blocks.caption: Helen Zille, chairwoman of the DA, has agreed to coalition talks with the ANC beforeImage: DW

blocks.text: The election results therefore signal a broader shift in South African politics, with voter support increasingly spread across multiple parties rather than being concentrated behind a single dominant force.

While nationally, the ANC remained the country's largest party, opposition parties made significant gains; the Democratic Alliance (DA) managed to strengthen its position across several major urban centers.

Meanwhile the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party, launched by former President Jacob Zuma in late 2023, performed rather strongly in the KwaZulu-Natal provice despite entering the political arena so recently.
At the local level, smaller civic organizations and community-based movements also recorded notable successes.
'Vote fluidity' enters South African politics
Essop describes this trend as a growing sense of "vote fluidity," with voters increasingly willing to move their support between parties instead of remaining loyal to a single political organization.

Some observers have already linked this drift to the idea of South Africans are moving beyond liberation-era loyalties; however, Essop opines: "I would be cautious to say that liberation politics are dead and gone," as many political parties continue to draw ther legitimacy and support from the country's liberation history — even if they no longer operate under the ANC banner.
Essop argues that the political shift does not signify a wholesale rejection of that liberation narrative itself, but rather a growing demand for effective governance and leadership.
A critical test for the ANC

For the ANC, the challenge now is rebuilding trust, with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa saying that the results are a challenge not just for his party but for all political parties to come together and perform better for citizens.
In a statement, Ramaphosa said that "[t]hose who have been elected to councils now need to prove themselves worthy of the trust placed in them by the South African people."

blocks.caption: The election results also represent a growing lack in confidence in Preseident Cyril Ramaphosa's leadershipImage: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: While the ANC still remains South Africa's largest political party, its latest setbacks at the polls underscore how much the country's political landscape is no longer what it was when apartheid ended.
The era of undisputed ANC loyalty and dominance appears to be over as voters are showing a greater willingness to support alternative parties and punish those they believe have fallen short.
Whether the ANC can reverse this decline will depend largely on how convincingly it can deliver not only improved public services, but effective change throughout.
